transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: Help! My pan of cooking oil caught fire on the stove at {location}! Flames are everywhere!

options.text: Turn off the stove and cover the pan with a metal lid to smother the flames.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: This is the safest immediate action.

options.text: Turn off the stove and use a fire blanket if you have one.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: This keeps everyone safe.

options.text: Pour water on the pan to extinguish it.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Water hits hot oil, vaporizes instantly, and causes a massive fireball that spreads the burning grease.

options.text: Blow hard on the flames to put them out.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Blowing on the flames feeds the fire with oxygen and can blow burning oil onto yourself or the kitchen.

options.text: Carry the burning pan outside.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Moving a burning pan causes the oil to slosh, dripping liquid fire on yourself and spreading it through the house.

options.text: Throw flour or sugar on the flames.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Flour and sugar dust are highly flammable and can cause a violent dust explosion when thrown into a fire.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: Okay! I covered it and turned off the stove. The flames stopped but there is smoke.

options.text: Leave the house now, close doors behind you, and wait outside for BFP.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Good advice for waiting on responders.

options.text: Evacuate everyone and stay outside until the fire truck arrives.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Keeps the caller safe while help arrives.

options.text: Open all windows to let the smoke out.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Opening windows introduces fresh oxygen that feeds the fire and creates a draft, spreading it faster.

options.text: Lift the lid to check if the fire is really out.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Lifting the lid reintroduces oxygen, which can cause the superheated oil to immediately reignite.

options.text: Pour water everywhere to cool the stove.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Pouring water near a grease fire risks spreading the grease or causing an electrical short circuit.

options.text: You don't need to evacuate, just stay inside.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Staying inside a burning structure exposes you to toxic smoke inhalation, which is the leading cause of fire deaths.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: Help! I'm at an apartment at {location}. Huge fire, smoke everywhere, people screaming!

options.text: Stay below the smoke and crawl to the nearest fire exit.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: This is the safest immediate action.

options.text: Stay inside your unit, seal the door gaps with a wet cloth, signal from window.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: This keeps everyone safe.

options.text: Take the elevator down to escape faster.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Elevators can fail during fires, trapping you inside a smoke-filled shaft and causing suffocation.

options.text: Open all doors and windows to let fresh air in.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Opening doors and windows creates drafts that pull the fire and smoke directly into your room.

options.text: Go up to the roof to wait for a helicopter.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Smoke and heat rise. The roof becomes incredibly toxic and hot, and helicopter rescues are extremely rare.

options.text: Run through the smoke as fast as you can.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Running through smoke increases breathing rate, leading to rapid toxic smoke inhalation and fainting.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: There is thick black smoke in the hallway! I cannot see the stairs.

options.text: Seal the door gap with wet cloth, stay low, signal from window.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Good advice for waiting on responders.

options.text: Block the door gap and stay near the window for air. BFP is coming.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Keeps the caller safe while help arrives.

options.text: Try to run through the smoke now while you can.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Running through smoke increases breathing rate, causing rapid carbon monoxide poisoning and fainting.

options.text: Break the window to get more air.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Breaking a window prevents you from closing it to block smoke later, and draws the fire towards your room.

options.text: Pour water under the door and open it.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Opening a hot door will let in superheated toxic smoke and flames, instantly overwhelming you.

options.text: Go out and knock on neighbors' doors.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Going into a smoke-filled hallway is deadly. Call 911 to alert them of your neighbors instead.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: Help! My husband was grinding metal at {location} and sparks ignited a workbench soaked with motor oil!

options.text: Do not use water! Cut main power if safe, and evacuate immediately.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: This is the safest immediate action.

options.text: Use a dry chemical extinguisher if you can reach it safely, otherwise evacuate.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: This keeps everyone safe.

options.text: Use a garden hose on the workbench right now.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Water conducts electricity. Spraying water on power tools will cause a severe electrical shock.

options.text: Open the garage doors wide to push the smoke out.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Opening a large garage door floods the fire with oxygen, causing it to explode in size.

options.text: Unplug the power tools one by one.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Approaching burning power tools puts you at risk of electrocution and severe burns.

options.text: Smother the oil fire with a blanket.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Using a regular blanket on a large oil fire can catch the blanket on fire and spread the burning oil.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: He got out! He is outside now. But the fire is growing fast.

options.text: Keep everyone outside and at least 10 meters away.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Good advice for waiting on responders.

options.text: Make sure no one goes back in. Move gas tanks away if safe to do from distance.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Keeps the caller safe while help arrives.

options.text: Go back inside to save your tools.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Tools are replaceable; your life is not. Toxic smoke in a garage contains lethal chemicals from plastics and oils.

options.text: Try to close the burning garage door.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Touching a burning door can cause severe burns, and staying near the fire exposes you to toxic smoke.

options.text: Pour buckets of water through the window.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Water on electrical or chemical fires will spread the fire or cause electrocution.

options.text: Call a neighbor to bring their garden hose.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Delaying evacuation to fight the fire puts both you and your neighbor in severe danger.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: Help! I'm on the 14th floor at {location}. The hallway is filled with thick smoke!

options.text: Stay inside with the door closed. Seal the gap with wet towels if it's not hot.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: This is the safest immediate action.

options.text: Do not go into the smoke-filled hallway. Stay inside and signal from window.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: This keeps everyone safe.

options.text: Run through the smoke to the stairwell.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Moving through thick smoke without visibility leads to disorientation, toxic inhalation, and death.

options.text: Take the elevator down.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Elevator shafts act as chimneys during a fire, filling with toxic smoke and trapping occupants.

options.text: Break the window to climb out to the ledge.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Climbing onto a ledge risks a fatal fall and exposes you to flames shooting out from lower windows.

options.text: Open the door wide to let the smoke flow through.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Opening a door provides oxygen to the fire and creates a draft, pulling flames and smoke directly into the room.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: Okay, I am inside. I put a wet towel under the door.

options.text: Wave a bright cloth from your window so firefighters can see you.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Good advice for waiting on responders.

options.text: Keep signaling from the window. Firefighters will come to you.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Keeps the caller safe while help arrives.

options.text: Try to rope down using bedsheets.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Bedsheets are not strong enough to hold human weight reliably, leading to fatal falls.

options.text: Open the window fully and breathe deeply.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Opening the window can pull smoke from other floors into your apartment. Only open slightly if necessary.

options.text: Leave the unit and try the stairwell again.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: If the stairwell is full of smoke, entering it is a fatal mistake due to toxic gases.

options.text: Pour water on the door and push through the smoke.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Opening the door to a fire-involved hallway will cause a backdraft or expose you to lethal heat.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: Help! I'm at a restaurant at {location}. The deep fryer flashed over to the ceiling!

options.text: Get everyone out of the kitchen and dining area immediately. Close doors behind you.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: This is the safest immediate action.

options.text: Activate the fire suppression system under the hood, then evacuate.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: This keeps everyone safe.

options.text: Keep trying to smother the fryer with towels.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Dry towels will quickly catch fire. If the fire is too large, trying to smother it puts you at severe burn risk.

options.text: Open all doors and windows to clear smoke for customers.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Opening doors feeds the fire oxygen and draws the smoke and flames into the customer area.

options.text: Send someone back in for the cash register.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: No amount of money is worth risking death from toxic smoke inhalation or structural collapse.

options.text: Pour water on the hot oil fryer.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Water vaporizes instantly when it hits hot oil, creating a massive fireball that spreads the burning grease.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: Everyone is out! We are at the front of the building.

options.text: Stay outside. Do not let anyone go back in. BFP is on the way.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Good advice for waiting on responders.

options.text: Make sure all customers stay far from the entrance.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Keeps the caller safe while help arrives.

options.text: Go back in to grab the fire extinguisher.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: If you are already out, going back inside a burning building is fatal due to rapidly accumulating toxic smoke.

options.text: Use a garden hose to spray through the front window.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Spraying water from outside can push the fire deeper into the building or create dangerous steam burns.

options.text: Send one staff back in to check if it's safe.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Never send anyone back into a burning building; the environment is highly toxic and unpredictable.

options.text: Try to turn off the gas line inside the kitchen.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Re-entering a burning kitchen to turn off the gas puts you in the direct path of the fire and potential explosions.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: Help! At a pool in {location}, two chemicals mixed and are releasing thick yellow gas!

options.text: Tell everyone to move upwind immediately, at least 50 meters away.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: This is the safest immediate action.

options.text: Move everyone upwind, cover mouths with wet cloth, do not touch anything.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: This keeps everyone safe.

options.text: Pour sand over the mixture.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Pouring sand on an unknown chemical mixture can cause a violent reactive explosion or release toxic gas.

options.text: Flood the spill with water.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Many chemicals react violently with water, boiling instantly, exploding, or releasing deadly fumes.

options.text: Use a fan to blow the gas away.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: A fan's electrical motor can spark and ignite flammable chemical fumes, causing an explosion.

options.text: Drag the chemical buckets outside.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Moving burning or reactive chemicals can spill them, spread the fire, or expose the caller to toxic and lethal fumes.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: We moved everyone upwind. Some are still coughing.

options.text: Stay where you are upwind. HazMat unit is dispatched.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Good advice for waiting on responders.

options.text: Keep people at a safe distance. Note anyone with breathing difficulty.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Keeps the caller safe while help arrives.

options.text: Go back and close the shed door.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Re-entering an area with chemical fumes can cause instant respiratory failure or loss of consciousness.

options.text: Have someone go back to read the chemical labels.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Sending someone into a toxic environment is deadly. Wait for HazMat equipped with breathing apparatus.

options.text: Rinse eyes in the pool water.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Pool water contains chlorine which can further react with the chemical in the eyes, causing blindness.

options.text: Ventilate the shed by opening panels.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Opening panels can expose the chemicals to moisture in the air or oxygen, escalating the reaction.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: Help! A power line snapped at {location}. It's sparking on wet grass and burning!

options.text: Tell everyone to back away 10 meters and do not touch wet ground.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: This is the safest immediate action.

options.text: Warn bystanders that electricity travels through wet ground. Stay back.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: This keeps everyone safe.

options.text: Use a wooden stick to drag the wire off the road.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Even wood can conduct high-voltage electricity if slightly damp, resulting in a fatal shock.

options.text: Throw sand on the wire.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Approaching a live high-voltage wire to throw anything puts you within the arc flash zone, risking electrocution.

options.text: Gather bystanders under a nearby roof.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Gathering people near an electrical incident is unsafe; a wire snap or arc can strike from a distance.

options.text: Use a garden hose to wet down the grass.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Using a garden hose is ineffective against a spreading fire and delays evacuation, endangering the caller's life.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: Okay, I told everyone to back away.

options.text: Do not fight the fire. Keep everyone away. Meralco/BFP will handle it.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Good advice for waiting on responders.

options.text: Keep everyone away and clear the road.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Keeps the caller safe while help arrives.

options.text: Throw water on the burning grass.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Throwing water near a downed live wire will conduct electricity back to you, causing electrocution.

options.text: Cut the wire from the pole with insulated tools.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Only trained utility workers have the proper equipment to handle high-voltage lines. Standard tools will fail.

options.text: Stomp out the grass fire.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Stomping near a downed power line puts your body in the path of stray electrical currents traveling through the ground.

options.text: Move the metal fence away from the wire.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Metal conducts electricity perfectly. Touching a metal fence near a downed wire is instantly fatal.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: Help! A cooking stall at the market in {location} is on fire near LPG tanks!

options.text: Evacuate everyone at least 50 meters away immediately.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: This is the safest immediate action.

options.text: Do not try to move the LPG tanks. Get everyone away now.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: This keeps everyone safe.

options.text: Try to drag the LPG tanks out of the fire.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: LPG tanks in a fire can rupture and cause a BLEVE (Boiling Liquid Expanding Vapor Explosion), which is instantly lethal.

options.text: Throw buckets of water on the LPG tanks to cool them.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Approaching burning LPG tanks puts you in the immediate blast radius if they explode.

options.text: Run into the stall to save the cash box.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Entering a burning stall surrounded by LPG tanks is extremely dangerous due to the risk of an explosion.

options.text: Use a blanket to smother the LPG tank.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: A blanket will not stop pressurized LPG from leaking and can trap gas, leading to a massive explosion.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: We evacuated the area. The fire is huge.

options.text: Keep everyone far away behind solid cover if possible.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Good advice for waiting on responders.

options.text: Do not let anyone return to their stalls.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Keeps the caller safe while help arrives.

options.text: Go back to see if the tanks are expanding.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: If a tank is expanding, it is seconds away from a massive explosion. You must stay far away.

options.text: Spray water from a nearby hose onto the flames.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Using a garden hose requires you to get too close to pressurized tanks that could explode at any moment.

options.text: Start moving nearby stalls away from the fire.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Moving stalls wastes time and keeps you in the danger zone. Evacuate immediately.

options.text: Try to turn the LPG tank valves off.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Reaching into a fire to turn off a valve exposes you to severe burns and potential explosion.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: Help! There is a chemical fire in the science lab at {location}!

options.text: Activate the fire alarm and evacuate via the nearest marked exit.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: This is the safest immediate action.

options.text: Evacuate the classroom immediately, leaving all belongings behind.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: This keeps everyone safe.

options.text: Throw water on the chemical fire.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Water spreads chemical fires and can cause explosive reactions with certain substances.

options.text: Try to identify the burning chemicals before leaving.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Inhaling burning chemical smoke for even a few seconds can be immediately fatal.

options.text: Use the classroom curtains to smother the flames.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Curtains are highly flammable and will catch fire, spreading the flames to the rest of the room.

options.text: Run out and open all windows to let the smoke out.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Opening windows introduces fresh oxygen, which will feed the fire and cause it to spread rapidly.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: The fire alarm is ringing and we are outside.

options.text: Gather at the designated assembly point outside.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Good advice for waiting on responders.

options.text: Do not re-enter the building for any reason.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Keeps the caller safe while help arrives.

options.text: Go back to get your backpacks.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: No belongings are worth dying for. Toxic smoke fills a room rapidly and can trap you.

options.text: Wait in the hallway outside the lab.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Hallways near a fire fill with smoke quickly. You must evacuate the building entirely.

options.text: Try to fight the fire from the doorway.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Fighting a chemical fire without proper extinguishers and training exposes you to lethal toxic fumes.

options.text: Go to the principal's office to report it.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Delaying evacuation to report in person puts you in danger. Pull the alarm and call 911 from outside.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: Help! A jeepney engine caught fire on the highway at {location}!

options.text: Get all passengers out and move far away from the vehicle.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: This is the safest immediate action.

options.text: Evacuate the jeepney and do not open the hood.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: This keeps everyone safe.

options.text: Open the hood to see where the fire is.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Opening the hood introduces a rush of oxygen that will cause the engine fire to erupt into a massive fireball.

options.text: Pour water on the engine block.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Water on a grease, oil, or fuel fire will spread the burning fuel and cause a massive flare-up.

options.text: Stay in the jeepney until the fire truck arrives.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Vehicles contain highly flammable fuels and plastics. Staying inside ensures you will be overcome by toxic smoke.

options.text: Try to restart the engine to blow out the fire.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Attempting to restart a burning engine will pump more fuel into the fire, worsening the explosion risk.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: Everyone is out of the jeepney.

options.text: Stay far away from the road and oncoming traffic.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Good advice for waiting on responders.

options.text: Warn oncoming traffic if safe to do so from a distance.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Keeps the caller safe while help arrives.

options.text: Go back to get your belongings from the jeepney.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Vehicle fires spread incredibly fast. Re-entering puts you at risk of being trapped by the flames.

options.text: Try to push the jeepney off the road.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Pushing a burning vehicle keeps you dangerously close to the fuel tank, which can explode.

options.text: Flag down other cars to use their fire extinguishers.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Stopping traffic near a burning vehicle creates secondary crash hazards and delays the fire department.

options.text: Stand next to the jeepney to take a video.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Standing near a burning vehicle exposes you to toxic fumes and potential shrapnel from exploding tires or struts.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: Help! There's a massive brush fire spreading towards the subdivision at {location}!

options.text: Stay inside, close all windows, and prepare to evacuate if ordered.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: This is the safest immediate action.

options.text: Turn off air conditioning to avoid drawing smoke in, stay inside.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: This keeps everyone safe.

options.text: Go out and start spraying your roof with a garden hose.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Spraying your roof delays your evacuation. If a wildfire is close, you must leave immediately.

options.text: Drive out into the smoke to see how close the fire is.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Driving into thick smoke causes you to lose visibility, crash, and become trapped by the approaching fire.

options.text: Start burning back-fires in your yard to stop the main fire.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Starting unauthorized fires will simply spread the fire faster and engulf your own property.

options.text: Evacuate immediately through the thick smoke.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Moving through thick smoke can cause fatal smoke inhalation; stay low under the smoke or shelter in place if trapped.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: We are inside our house, all windows closed.

options.text: Listen to local authorities and evacuate only when instructed.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Good advice for waiting on responders.

options.text: Keep a go-bag ready and wait for further instructions.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Keeps the caller safe while help arrives.

options.text: Go out and take pictures of the fire.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Wildfires move faster than you can run. Stopping to take pictures can trap you in the blaze.

options.text: Open the windows to see the fire better.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Opening windows allows flying embers to enter your home, igniting the inside immediately.

options.text: Try to fight the fire with a garden hose.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: A garden hose is useless against a massive wildfire and attempting to use it will cost you your life.

options.text: Ignore the fire, it won't reach you.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Wildfires are completely unpredictable and can change direction in seconds. Always follow evacuation warnings.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: Emergency at {location}! My dad is choking on a pork bone! He's turning blue and can't speak!

options.text: Perform abdominal thrusts (Heimlich maneuver) immediately.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Correct medical procedure.

options.text: Stand behind him, make a fist above his navel, and pull inward and upward.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Best action to stabilize the patient.

options.text: Give him a glass of water to wash it down.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Giving water to a choking victim can force the object deeper into the airway.

options.text: Slap him hard on the back while he is standing upright.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Slapping the back of an upright choking adult can cause the object to lodge deeper in the airway.

options.text: Try to reach into his throat with your fingers to pull it out.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: A blind finger sweep can push the obstruction further down the throat, completely blocking the airway.

options.text: Tell him to lie down and rest.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Lying down does not clear the airway and the person will suffocate if the object is not removed.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: Okay, I'm doing the Heimlich maneuver now.

options.text: Keep doing thrusts until the object is dislodged or he goes unconscious.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Good instruction while waiting for paramedics.

options.text: If he passes out, lay him flat and start CPR. The ambulance is coming.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Keeps the patient stable.

options.text: Stop doing thrusts and just wait for the ambulance.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Stopping abdominal thrusts allows the patient to suffocate. You must continue until the object is clear.

options.text: Try pouring water down his throat now.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Pouring water will go into the lungs or push the object deeper, causing further choking.

options.text: Leave him alone, he'll cough it up eventually.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: If the airway is fully blocked, they cannot cough and will pass out and die without intervention.

options.text: Try the finger sweep again.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Blind finger sweeps often push the object deeper. Only remove an object if it is clearly visible.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: Emergency at {location}! My coworker fell from a ladder and his leg has bright red blood spurting out!

options.text: Apply firm, direct pressure on the wound with a clean cloth.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Correct medical procedure.

options.text: Apply direct pressure and consider using a tourniquet high above the wound if it won't stop.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Best action to stabilize the patient.

options.text: Try to splint the leg first to keep it straight.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Attempting to splint without proper training can cause further nerve or vascular damage.

options.text: Wash the wound with water to clean it.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Washing a severe wound washes away clotting blood and accelerates life-threatening blood loss.

options.text: Elevate the leg but do not apply pressure.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Elevation without direct pressure is not enough to stop severe arterial bleeding.

options.text: Remove the shirt to check if it stopped bleeding.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Removing the cloth disrupts the blood clots that are forming, causing the severe bleeding to restart.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: I'm pressing hard on the wound with a clean shirt.

options.text: Keep continuous pressure. Do not lift the cloth to check.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Good instruction while waiting for paramedics.

options.text: Do not release the pressure until paramedics arrive.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Keeps the patient stable.

options.text: Take the cloth off to let it breathe.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Letting a severe wound 'breathe' will simply allow it to bleed out. Continuous pressure is required.

options.text: Try to walk him to a car to drive to the hospital.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Walking increases the heart rate and blood pressure, causing the wound to bleed out much faster.

options.text: Give him water to drink.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Giving water to trauma patients can cause them to vomit, risking aspiration, or complicate emergency surgery.

options.text: Apply a loose bandage and wait.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: A loose bandage will not stop severe bleeding. Firm, direct pressure is critical to save their life.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: Emergency at {location}! A teenager is shaking violently on the ground, his eyes are rolled back!

options.text: Clear any hard objects away from him and let the seizure run its course.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Correct medical procedure.

options.text: Do not restrain him. Protect his head with something soft.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Best action to stabilize the patient.

options.text: Hold his arms down so he stops shaking.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Restraining someone during a seizure can lead to bone fractures or muscle tears.

options.text: Put a spoon in his mouth so he doesn't bite his tongue.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Placing objects in the mouth can break their teeth, cause choking, or cause severe jaw injuries.

options.text: Splash water on his face to wake him up.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Splashing water will not stop a seizure and could cause them to inhale the water and choke.

options.text: Try to sit him up.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Sitting them up during a seizure can cause airway restriction or result in falls and head injuries.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: I moved the chairs away. He is still shaking.

options.text: Time the seizure. When it stops, roll him onto his side.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Good instruction while waiting for paramedics.

options.text: Stay with him and gently turn him on his side once the shaking stops.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Keeps the patient stable.

options.text: Try to give him medicine while he's shaking.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Attempting to give medicine during a seizure will cause them to choke and block their airway.

options.text: Pin him to the floor to keep him still.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Restraining a seizing person can cause severe muscle tearing, joint dislocations, or bone fractures.

options.text: Slap his face to snap him out of it.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Slapping someone having a seizure will not stop the neurological event and only causes physical abuse.

options.text: Leave him there and go wait outside for the ambulance.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Leaving a seizing patient unattended puts them at risk of head injury or choking on their own fluids.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: Emergency at {location}! My grandma's face is drooping on one side and her speech is slurred!

options.text: Keep her seated safely and note exactly what time the symptoms started.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Correct medical procedure.

options.text: Do not give her any food, water, or aspirin. Keep her calm.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Best action to stabilize the patient.

options.text: Give her an aspirin immediately to thin her blood.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Giving aspirin without diagnosing the type of stroke (ischemic vs hemorrhagic) can cause fatal bleeding if it is a hemorrhagic stroke.

options.text: Have her walk around to get the blood flowing.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Walking forces the heart to work harder, which can be fatal during a heart attack or stroke.

options.text: Give her a glass of water.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: A stroke victim may have lost the ability to swallow properly and could easily choke on the water.

options.text: Have her lie flat on her back.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Lying flat can cause airway blockage if they vomit or lose consciousness. Seated or recovery position is safer.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: She is sitting safely in a chair now.

options.text: Keep her calm and reassure her help is on the way.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Good instruction while waiting for paramedics.

options.text: Monitor her breathing and stay on the line with me.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Keeps the patient stable.

options.text: Try to feed her something sweet.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Feeding someone having a stroke can cause them to choke as they may not be able to swallow.

options.text: Have her go to sleep.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Letting a stroke victim sleep prevents you from monitoring their consciousness and breathing.

options.text: Try to drive her to the hospital yourself.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Driving her yourself means she won't receive life-saving medical interventions en route in the ambulance.

options.text: Give her her blood pressure medication.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Giving medication without medical direction during a stroke can fatally alter their blood pressure.

transcript.text: Emergency at {location}! My friend ate shellfish and now his lips are swollen and he's wheezing!

options.text: Use the EpiPen on his outer thigh and monitor his breathing.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Best action to stabilize the patient.

options.text: Give him water to clear his throat.

options.explanation: Giving water to someone having an allergic reaction or airway swelling can cause them to choke.

options.text: Have him stand up and walk around to stay awake.

options.text: Give him a Benadryl pill and wait to see if he improves.
options.label: unsafe

options.text: Try to induce vomiting so he throws up the food.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Vomiting will not reverse the allergic reaction and risks stomach acid burning a swollen airway.

transcript.speaker: Caller

options.text: Keep him lying flat and monitor his breathing. Paramedics are coming.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Good instruction while waiting for paramedics.

options.text: If he stops breathing, begin CPR. Do not let him sit up suddenly.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Keeps the patient stable.

options.text: Have him sit upright so it's easier to breathe.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: While it helps breathing, sitting upright can cause fatal blood pressure drops during anaphylaxis; lying flat is safer.

options.text: Give him another EpiPen immediately.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Giving a second EpiPen too soon without medical direction can cause dangerous heart arrhythmias.

options.text: Offer him food to settle his stomach.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Giving food to someone with a swollen airway will cause them to choke and completely block the airway.

options.text: Leave him alone to rest.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Anaphylaxis is rapidly fatal without continuous monitoring and medical intervention.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: Emergency at {location}! My baby is unresponsive and not breathing!

options.text: Place the baby on a firm surface and begin infant CPR with two fingers on the chest.

options.label: safe
options.explanation: Best action to stabilize the patient.

options.text: Do adult CPR with both hands.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Using two hands for adult CPR on an infant is too forceful and can easily break their ribs or puncture their lungs.

options.text: Shake the baby to try and wake them up.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Shaking an infant can cause severe, permanent brain damage (Shaken Baby Syndrome) or death.

options.text: Turn the baby upside down and slap their back.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Turning an infant upside down can cause them to be dropped and slapping can cause internal injuries.

options.text: Wait for the ambulance before doing anything.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Delaying CPR significantly decreases survival chances; brain damage can occur within minutes without oxygen.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: Okay, I'm doing CPR with two fingers.

options.text: Keep doing CPR continuously until paramedics arrive.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Good instruction while waiting for paramedics.

options.text: Do not stop CPR. The ambulance is on its way.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Keeps the patient stable.

options.text: Stop CPR to check for a pulse every 10 seconds.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Could worsen the patient's condition.

options.text: Pick the baby up and rock them.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Rocking the baby does not provide the oxygen and blood circulation needed when they are not breathing.

options.text: Splash water on the baby's face.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Splashing water does not restart breathing and wastes critical time when CPR is needed immediately.

options.text: Give the baby milk.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Giving milk to an unresponsive infant will cause them to choke or aspirate fluid into their lungs.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: Emergency at {location}! We just pulled a man from the pool. He's not breathing!

options.text: Begin CPR immediately, starting with rescue breaths.

options.explanation: Correct medical procedure.

options.text: Start chest compressions and rescue breaths. 30 compressions, 2 breaths.

options.text: Turn him upside down to drain the water from his lungs.

options.text: Press on his stomach to force the water out.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Pressing the stomach forces water into the lungs or causes vomiting, which blocks the airway.

options.text: Leave him on his side and wait.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: If he is not breathing, leaving him on his side will result in death. CPR must begin immediately.

options.text: Slap his face to wake him up.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Slapping an unconscious drowning victim does not restore breathing and delays critical CPR.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: Okay, I'm starting CPR.

options.text: Continue CPR without stopping until the paramedics arrive.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Good instruction while waiting for paramedics.

options.text: If you have an AED nearby, turn it on and follow the voice prompts.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Keeps the patient stable.

options.text: Stop CPR if water comes out of his mouth.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: If water comes out, turn his head to drain it, then resume CPR immediately. Stopping CPR will cause death.

options.text: Try to find a doctor before starting CPR.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Every second counts in drowning. Waiting for a doctor before starting CPR ensures severe brain damage.

options.text: Roll him around to clear the water.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Rolling him around wastes time. Begin chest compressions and rescue breaths immediately to supply oxygen.

options.text: Give him mouth-to-mouth only, no compressions.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Chest compressions are essential to circulate the oxygenated blood to the brain and vital organs.

transcript.speaker: Caller

options.text: Try to sit him up and give him water.

transcript.text: I'm doing chest compressions hard and fast.

options.text: Keep going, don't stop. Push at a rate of 100 to 120 beats per minute.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Good instruction while waiting for paramedics.

options.text: Do not stop compressions until the paramedics take over.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Keeps the patient stable.

options.text: Stop CPR to see if he's breathing every few seconds.

options.text: Try mouth-to-mouth only.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Without chest compressions, the oxygen from mouth-to-mouth will not circulate to the brain.

options.text: Just wait, help is almost there.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Brain death occurs in 4-6 minutes without CPR. Waiting for help without acting is fatal.

options.text: Take his helmet off so he can breathe better.

options.label: unsafe

options.text: Drag him to the side of the road.

options.text: Give him water to drink.
options.label: unsafe

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: Okay, I won't touch him or his helmet.

options.text: Keep him still and reassure him that help is coming.

options.text: Do not move his neck or back. Wait for paramedics.

options.text: Try to move him out of the sun.

options.text: Take the helmet off to check for head bleeding.

options.text: Follow the direction they went to see if they dropped it.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Following the suspects puts you at risk of a dangerous confrontation if you catch up to them.

options.text: Tell the victim to go home.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: The victim needs to stay to provide a statement to the police and receive potential medical attention.

options.text: Post about it on Facebook before talking to police.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Posting online before an official report can spread misinformation and alert the suspects.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: Police! I'm following a drunk driver swerving all over the highway near {location}!

options.text: Do not confront the driver. Give me the plate number and pull over safely.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: This ensures caller safety.

options.text: Stop following the vehicle. Pull over and give me their direction of travel.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Best action for police situations.

options.text: Speed up and try to block their car.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Trying to block a reckless driver will likely cause a severe accident involving your vehicle.

options.text: Drive really close behind them to read the plate.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Tailgating an erratic driver drastically increases your chances of being involved in a collision.

options.text: Honk and flash your lights to get them to pull over.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Aggressive signaling can provoke road rage or cause a drunk driver to panic and crash.

options.text: Try to run them off the road.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Running someone off the road is highly illegal and incredibly dangerous for everyone involved.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: I've pulled over and stopped following them.

options.text: Stay pulled over. Officers are checking the area for the vehicle.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Good instruction while waiting for police.

options.text: Do not try to follow them further. The police have the description.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Keeps the caller safe and hidden.

options.text: Get back on the highway and try to find them again.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Re-entering traffic to hunt down a reckless driver puts you back in the danger zone.

options.text: Follow them at a safe distance.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Even at a distance, following a reckless driver keeps you near a highly unpredictable and dangerous situation.

options.text: Try to throw something at their car to wake them up.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Throwing objects at a moving vehicle is illegal and can easily cause a fatal crash.

options.text: Wait for them to crash and then help.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Failing to report the driver immediately allows them to potentially cause a fatal accident.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: Police! I work at a convenience store in {location}. There's an armed robbery happening now! I'm hiding behind the counter.

options.text: Stay hidden, stay completely silent, and do not try to stop them.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: This ensures caller safety.

options.text: Do not use any alarms that make noise. Stay out of sight.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Best action for police situations.

options.text: Stand up and tell them the police are on the way.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Revealing that police are coming can panic armed robbers, leading to a hostage situation or shooting.

options.text: Try to sneak up and tackle the robber.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Attacking an armed suspect unarmed is incredibly risky and can easily result in you or others being shot.

options.text: Throw something to distract them.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Sudden movements or thrown objects can startle an armed robber into pulling the trigger.

options.text: Run out the front door while they aren't looking.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Running makes you a visible target. If they notice you, they may shoot.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: I am staying hidden and quiet.

options.text: Keep hiding until the police arrive and secure the store.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Good instruction while waiting for police.

options.text: Do not move or make noise. The police are pulling up outside.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Keeps the caller safe and hidden.

options.text: Peek over the counter to see what they are doing.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Exposing your head makes you visible to the robbers, drawing their attention and potentially their fire.

options.text: Try to record a video with your phone with the flash on.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: The flash will instantly alert the robbers to your exact location, putting your life in immediate danger.

options.text: Yell for help.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Yelling draws the armed robbers' attention directly to you, making you a primary target.

options.text: Try to run to the back room while they are armed.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Moving while robbers are active increases your chances of being seen and shot. Staying still is safer.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: Police! My grandmother with dementia wandered off from {location} about 2 hours ago!

options.text: We will file a report immediately. Please check any nearby familiar landmarks.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: This ensures caller safety.

options.text: Stay at the location in case she returns. Officers are responding to help search.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Best action for police situations.

options.text: Wait another 24 hours before filing a report.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: The first 24 hours are the most critical in a missing person case. Delaying the report reduces the chances of a safe recovery.

options.text: Drive around randomly looking for her.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Random searching is inefficient and takes you away from the home, which is where she might return or call.

options.text: Assume she went to visit a friend and wait.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Making assumptions wastes valuable time. It is always better to involve the police early.

options.text: Don't worry, she will find her way back.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Dismissing the situation is dangerous, especially for vulnerable individuals who may be lost or injured.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: I've checked the immediate area, she's not here.

options.text: Gather a recent photo of her and list what she was wearing for the officers.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Good instruction while waiting for police.

options.text: Have her medical information ready for the police.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Keeps the caller safe and hidden.

options.text: Go out searching alone and leave the house empty.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Leaving the house empty means no one is there if she returns or calls the home phone.

options.text: Post a reward online before talking to police.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Posting rewards without police coordination can invite scammers and interfere with the official investigation.

options.text: Go check the hospitals yourself instead of waiting.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: The police can check hospital records much faster. Driving around wastes time and leaves your home unattended.

options.text: Assume she took a bus out of town.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Guessing her movements without evidence delays the actual search efforts in the immediate area.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: Police! There was a stabbing outside the barangay hall in {location}! The victim is bleeding badly.

options.text: Apply firm pressure around the wound, but do not remove the weapon if it is embedded.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: This ensures caller safety.

options.text: Keep pressure on the bleeding, but leave the knife exactly where it is.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Best action for police situations.

options.text: Pull the knife out immediately so it doesn't cause more damage.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Pulling an impaled object out removes the 'plug' holding the blood in, which can cause immediate, fatal bleeding.

options.text: Wash the wound with alcohol.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Alcohol damages exposed tissue and does not stop bleeding. It only causes unnecessary severe pain.

options.text: Try to move the victim inside the hall.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Moving a victim with an impaled object can shift the blade, slicing arteries or organs and worsening the injury.

options.text: Leave the victim alone until police arrive.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Leaving a severe bleeding victim alone can result in them bleeding to death before help arrives.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: I'm applying pressure around the wound. The weapon is still in his arm.

options.text: Keep applying pressure. Do not touch or remove the weapon. Police and EMTs are coming.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Good instruction while waiting for police.

options.text: Maintain pressure and try to keep the victim calm.
options.label: safe
options.explanation: Keeps the caller safe and hidden.

options.text: Try to pull the weapon out just a little bit.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Any movement of the weapon can cause further internal damage and increase bleeding.

options.text: Remove the pressure to see if it stopped bleeding.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Releasing pressure allows blood clots to break, causing the severe bleeding to resume immediately.

options.text: Try to walk the victim to a car.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Walking increases heart rate, which pumps blood faster out of the wound, accelerating blood loss.

options.text: Give the victim some water to drink.
options.label: unsafe
options.explanation: Giving water to someone with severe trauma can cause vomiting or complications if they need emergency surgery.
